html:
The Mandan are a Native American people of the upper Missouri River in what is now North Dakota. They speak a Siouan language and have lived along the Missouri, the Heart and the Knife rivers for centuries.

They were farmers and traders. Their towns of large round earth lodges, each home to a family traced through the mother's line, stood around a central plaza. Their corn surpluses made their villages, with those of the Hidatsa and Arikara, the great trade market of the northern Plains, where nomads brought meat, hides and later horses and guns.

The Lewis and Clark Expedition spent the winter of 1804 to 1805 beside the Mandan, and there hired Sacagawea and her husband. The painter George Catlin recorded their life in 1832. Five years later smallpox killed most of the Mandan. The survivors joined the Hidatsa and Arikara, and today they are part of the Three Affiliated Tribes at Fort Berthold.
